audit_findings.title: The cash bridge may add operating float as surplus cash
audit_findings.magnitude: $924.411 million bridge addition ($20.85 per share; 5.1% of base value); surplus portion unquantified
audit_findings.mechanism: Any cash required to fund contract liabilities, remaining project costs, collateral, or minimum operating liquidity should be excluded from the equity bridge.
audit_findings.evidence: As we worked through these upfront payments, we saw the expected decrease in operating cash as our cash outflows exceeded our inflows on these projects.
audit_findings.explanation: The filings demonstrate that customer advances finance working capital: net contract liabilities were $2.210 billion at June 30, 2026, versus $924.411 million of cash. This does not prove that none of the cash is distributable because contract liabilities are not equivalent to an immediately payable debt. The record does not identify the surplus portion, but the entire bridge addition is large enough to affect the valuation meaningfully, although removing all of it would reduce base value only from $407.90 to about $387.05 per share.
audit_findings.action: Reconcile cash to contract liabilities, remaining costs to complete, restricted cash, insurance collateral, acquisition commitments, and minimum operating liquidity; rerun the bridge using only demonstrably distributable excess cash.

audit_findings.title: Unfunded multiemployer pension claims are absent from the equity bridge
audit_findings.mechanism: A probable withdrawal liability or past-service underfunding claim would be deducted in the equity bridge; recurring surcharges would reduce normalized OE.
audit_findings.evidence: Our potential liability for unfunded liabilities could be material.
audit_findings.explanation: The filing confirms participation in approximately 200 plans, including red- and yellow-zone plans, and says withdrawal liability could be material. It also reports $341.910 million of 2025 multiemployer pension contributions, but that amount is an operating expense rather than a measure of the omitted liability. No material withdrawal liability was recorded, and the company states that amount and timing cannot be determined, so neither an error nor materiality is demonstrated.
audit_findings.action: Obtain plan-specific withdrawal-liability estimates, current funding ratios, rehabilitation-plan terms, employer concentration, and any triggering reductions in participation; deduct any probable net claim and rerun OE for recurring surcharges.

audit_findings.title: Recognized disputed claims weaken the cash quality of the OE anchor
audit_findings.magnitude: $116.1 million claims receivable, up $109.2 million; 9.5% and 8.9% of anchor OE, respectively
audit_findings.mechanism: Uncollectible or reversed claim revenue would reduce the OE anchor; treating a nonrecurring working-capital build as distributable earnings also overstates cash conversion.
audit_findings.evidence: There were $ 116.1 million and $ 6.9 million of claims included within accounts receivable as of December 31, 2025 and 2024, respectively.
audit_findings.explanation: The large recognized balance is demonstrated, but a loss is not: the filings do not disclose subsequent collections, settlements, or write-downs. The $116.1 million balance is 9.5% of the $1,221.6 million anchor and is therefore reasonably capable of materially changing the capitalized OE valuation if the anchor includes earnings that will not convert to cash.
audit_findings.action: Trace each claim through June 30, 2026 and subsequent resolution; reconcile recognized revenue, associated costs, cash collections, allowances, and reversals, then rerun the valuation using the sustainable after-tax OE or working-capital adjustment supported by that evidence.

audit_findings.title: The FY2025 numerator includes a business no longer owned
audit_findings.magnitude: $20.969 million 2025 UK segment operating income, equal to 1.7% of anchor OE; exact OE effect unquantified
audit_findings.mechanism: Eleven months of disposed UK earnings remain in the OE anchor even though the valuation-date equity owns only the sale proceeds reflected in subsequent cash.
audit_findings.evidence: On December 1, 2025, we sold our United Kingdom operations, the results of which are reported within our United Kingdom building services segment through the date of sale.
audit_findings.explanation: The perimeter mismatch is demonstrated. However, disclosed UK segment operating income was only $20.969 million, or 1.7% of the $1,221.6 million anchor, while UK revenue was about 2.8% of consolidated 2025 revenue. The exact OE contribution requires taxes, capital expenditure, amortization, and transaction-cost normalization, but the filed scale is not large enough to change the valuation conclusion.
audit_findings.action: Recast 2025 OE excluding UK operations through December 1, remove the $144.876 million disposal gain exactly once, normalize the $10.7 million sale costs, and confirm that net sale proceeds appear only through valuation-date cash.

audit_findings.title: Growth may require acquisition spending omitted from owner earnings
audit_findings.magnitude: $1.022105 billion of 2025 acquisition cash spending, equal to 83.7% of anchor OE, plus approximately $700 million of aggregate upfront acquisition price disclosed after June 30, 2026
audit_findings.mechanism: Acquisition spending required to sustain modeled growth is reinvestment that must reduce distributable OE or the growth assumption; adding back acquired-intangible amortization without replacement investment further inflates OE.
audit_findings.evidence: Our business strategy relies, in part, on acquisitions to sustain our growth, and these transactions present certain risks and uncertainties.
audit_findings.explanation: The filings demonstrate that acquisitions contribute to growth and that acquisition spending is very large relative to OE. They do not establish how much spending is recurring or necessary for the modeled 3% and 6% growth rates. Because 2025 acquisitions supplied approximately $1.27 billion of incremental revenue and the cash spending approached the full OE anchor, omission of required acquisition reinvestment is reasonably capable of materially overstating value.
audit_findings.action: Separate organic and acquired OE growth, identify all intangible-amortization addbacks, estimate maintenance acquisition spending needed to replace customer attrition or sustain each growth rate, and rerun every scenario with the corresponding reinvestment charge or acquisition-free growth rate.

audit_findings.title: The PEMEX casualty may leave an uninsured common-equity claim
audit_findings.mechanism: Any unreserved uninsured damages, deductibles, captive retention, defense costs, or denied recovery would reduce OE when incurred or require an equity-bridge deduction.
audit_findings.evidence: Based on currently available information, we believe insurance will cover much or all of any amounts required to be paid by Repcon or EIS in connection with these claims.
audit_findings.explanation: The casualty, fatalities, alleged injuries, lawsuits, indemnification claims, and mediation are demonstrated. Complete insurance recovery is not: management says insurance should cover “much or all.” The latest filing repeats the matter without a case-specific reserve, loss range, or coverage limit. Total net insurance liabilities of $330.4 million cannot be attributed to this case, so the record cannot establish its valuation magnitude.
audit_findings.action: Obtain the case-specific gross reserve, recorded net liability, policy limits, exclusions, deductibles, captive retention, defense-cost treatment, indemnification exposure, and insurer acceptance; rerun the bridge for any probable net claim not already recorded.
